paper_title: Movie2Game-Bench: Holistic Evaluation of Film-to-Game Adaptation Beyond Playability

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Adapting a film into a game requires selecting source elements and translating them into player actions, rules, and feedback. We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench), a benchmark for evaluating film-to-game adaptation beyond playability. M2G-bench combines general evaluation, movie-specific evaluation, and playtesting by three GUI model players. The protocol connects source content to gameplay steps and implementation evidence, capturing both content preservation and interactive realization. The benchmark comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. Evaluating 14 models on the same films with their selected primary harnesses reveals complementary strengths in game quality, adaptation, and player experience. A shared weakness concerns playable sequences: this category has the lowest content-presence mean in all 14 models, averaging 37.9 out of 100 compared with 54.8 for iconic elements. Among judgments of retained emotionaldevelopment content, narrative choices account for 60.0% and scenario operation for 7.2%. These findings identify two linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation: preserving source situations that can support gameplay and connecting retained content to player actions and consequences.

Introduction film can become detective game, driving challenge, or an interactive narrative. Each adaptation makes choice about what the player should do with the source material. Recognizing character, reproducing location, and turning conflict into consequential action are distinct achievements. Evaluating film-to-game generation therefore requires connecting the source film to the generated work and to the players experience of that work. These advances establish foundation for studying adaptation. film, however, supplies narrative events and audiovisual situations rather than an executable specification of game rules. The adaptation problem is to select meaningful source content and realize it through playable design. The same scene can support multiple valid mechanics, so evaluation needs source reference that accommodates differences in implementation. 1 We introduce Movie2Game-Bench (M2G-bench) for holistic evaluation of film-to-game adaptation  (Fig. 1)  . General Evaluation assesses Playability, Gameplay, and Presentation. Movie-specific Evaluation distinguishes sourcecontent presence from interactive realization. Playtesting records three GUI model players actions and experience. Together, these perspectives reveal how game functions, what it preserves from the film, and how players engage with it. The protocol traces source content into player interaction. Film-specific reference items cover plot, character relationships, iconic elements, playable sequences, and emotional development. Evaluators connect each items realization to game content, gameplay steps, and implementation evidence. Retaining chase as text and letting player control movement through it express different relationships to the source. The protocol records this difference while accommodating narrative choices, puzzles, and action mechanics. M2G-bench comprises 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items. We evaluate 14 models in their selected primary harnesses, averaging each score over all 22 films with zero for unsuccessful generation. Astra has the highest General Evaluation, Playtesting, and Overall means; Gemini has the highest Movie-specific mean. All 14 models preserve playable sequences less fully than the other four reference categories, identifying shared gap in retaining source situations that could ground gameplay. Item-level analysis then examines how retained plot, playable sequences, and emotional development are expressed through different forms of player participation. Our contributions are: full-film adaptation benchmark with 22 films and 658 source-specific reference items, supporting open game designs under common browser-game task. holistic evaluation protocol that connects general game quality, movie-specific adaptation, and playtesting through traceable source, code, and gameplay evidence. Evidence of shared content-preservation gap in playable sequences across all 14 models, complemented by analysis of the operation forms used to express retained film content. 2. Related Work Interactive worlds and game creation. Genie learns controllable environments from unlabelled video [3]; GameNGen simulates real-time game engine through diffusion [32]; and GameGen-X generates game videos with interactive control [5]. Film adaptation adds semantic design problem: reorganizing source narrative around player actions in an executable game. GameDevBench evaluates tutorial-derived development 2 tasks [8], and OpenGameEval checks edited scenes and simulated play in Roblox Studio [31]. GameCraft-Bench evaluates complete game construction through runtime replay, mechanics, content, and presentation [17]. CEGameBench covers five engines with real-input play verification [11]. Harness-of-Harness organizes coding agents into iterative planning, coding, and testing loops, including game development [37]. These works establish executable artifacts and observed behavior as evaluation targets. M2Gbench adds full film as the source for designing content and interaction. Game quality and playtesting. GameXpert-Bench covers game generation, repair, and optimization, including visual quality and player experience [6]. GameASG-Bench uses declared interfaces and executable checks to assess generated software behavior [39]. M2G-bench combines general game-quality profile with evaluation of the adaptations relationship to its source film. Orak and LMGame-Bench evaluate game-playing agents across diverse games and examine agent modules [15, 24]. PlaytestArena uses independent GUI judges to test expected in-play behavior, while Play2Code incorporates playtester feedback into iterative game creation [16]. Our GUI players produce trajectories, screenshots, reports, and questionnaires that support game-quality and experience scores. Movie-specific Evaluation connects those interactions to source events and relationships. Source reconstruction, replication, and adaptation. Video2Game reconstructs interactive environments from video using explicit scene representations and simulation [35]. CineRecon evaluates editable dynamic-scene reconstruction from cinematic references [33]. Film adaptation permits changes in viewpoint, temporal organization, and interaction style, motivating reference inventory of meaningful source content. GameReplica studies the recovery of visual and behavioral properties of reference games [25], and SWE-Game evaluates development tasks derived from existing games, including reference-video conditions [7]. Such games supply target mechanics to reproduce; films supply events from which mechanics must be devised. RPGAgent coordinates narrative, spatial, and mechanical generation to turn story synopses into playable role-playing prototypes [38]. M2Gbench evaluates multiple systems conditioned on complete audiovisual films through common source-content inventory and actual gameplay evidence. understanding use. Long-video MovieChat addresses long-video understanding through long-context memory [27]; LongVideoBench studies content and video-language understanding [34]; and Video-MME evaluates multimodal video understanding [12]. Film-to-game adaptation makes downstream content use observable in persistent artifact: characters enter the game world and events become playable situations. M2G-bench evaluates this use through source-grounded content judgments, observed interaction, and player experience. 3. Movie2Game-Bench 3.1. Task and Source Reference The task is to adapt complete audiovisual film into self-contained browser game. The instruction leaves the game type and design to the generator. Each agent works unattended for up to three hours, with local development tools and model-service access. The game consists of an HTML entry point and bundled assets, served by static local server during evaluation. The environment provides no application backend or general Internet access. All systems receive the same task instruction and artifact contract. The film collection contains 22 titles spanning different periods, languages, and audiovisual forms, including silent films, dialogue-centered dramas, animation, and action films. The collection supports different adaptation opportunities: investigating evidence, coordinating characters, controlling movement, and organizing resources. These opportunities motivate the film selection while leaving the generated gameplay open. The complete film list and reference-item counts appear in Tab. S3; screenshots of generated adaptations appear in Sec. D. Each film is associated with fixed inventory of sourcespecific reference items. The 658 items cover five categories: plot structure, characters and relationships, iconic elements, playable sequences, and emotional development. Most films have 30 items; two have 29. An item names content to check in an adaptation and includes source grounding. It does not prescribe unique interface or mechanic. For example, an evidence-related plot item can be expressed through inspecting objects, comparing testimony, or choosing line of inquiry. Reference construction uses timestamped frame grids, visual records, and dialogue transcripts. Six independent extractions, organized as generalist and specialist roles, identify candidate items. merger groups candidates that address the same content within category and selects representative statements. Timestamp checks and dialogue verification ground the resulting inventory in the film. The inventory is fixed before the adaptation judgments and enters the evaluation stage separately from the generators instruction. This gives all systems common source reference while preserving their freedom to choose playable design. 3.2. Primary Systems We evaluate 14 models, listed in Tab. 1. Claude Opus and Sonnet use Claude Code [1] as their primary harness; GPT6-Astra and GPT-6.1-Sol use Codex [21]. Complementary System Strengths Table 1 compares 14 primary systems on the same 22 films. Astra has the highest General Evaluation mean at 82.0 and Playtesting mean at 59.0. Gemini has the highest Moviespecific mean at 36.0. Astra and Sol achieve Overall means of 55.4 and 55.2, respectively, through different combina6 tions of game quality and source-specific realization. Kimi ranks third in General and Playtesting and ninth in Movie-specific Evaluation; Gemini ranks first in Moviespecific Evaluation, tenth in General, and eighth in Playtesting. These profiles distinguish broad game quality from adaptation-specific achievement, exposing capabilities that an Overall ranking alone would obscure. Evaluation consistency. The two Movie-specific evaluators correlate at = 0.91 (Sec. C.4). Across 100 blind human playthroughs by ten participants, mean model-player scores correlate with human scores at Spearman ρ = 0.60 and average 11.1 points higher. Participants rated the games without access to model-player scores (Sec. C.5). 5.2. Preservation of Source Content Figure 4 compares content presence across the five sourcereference categories. Each thin line follows one models means over the same 22 films, with zero for unsuccessful generation. Playable sequences have the lowest mean within every one of the 14 models. Averaging models equally gives 37.9 for playable sequences, compared with 54.4 for plot, 54.8 for iconic elements, 52.8 for emotional development, and 46.0 for characters and relationships. Playable-sequence references describe concrete source situations that can support player actions. Their lower presence scores identify shared weakness in preserving these situations in the generated adaptation. Plot and recognizable film elements receive greater coverage, while the sequences that could ground gameplay are less fully retained. Figure 4 locates this gap at the level of content presence. Figure 5 then examines the operation forms used for content that is retained, connecting what enters an adaptation to how players engage with it. These are frequencies among retained-content judgments pooled across both evaluators; the operation forms describe implementation independently of the interaction score. Detailed costs, tokens, and runtimes appear in Tab. S10. 6. Conclusion M2G-bench evaluates game quality, source-specific adaptation, and player experience. Across 22 films, these perspectives reveal complementary model strengths. Playable sequences have the lowest content-presence mean within all 14 models, identifying shared gap in preserving source situations that can support gameplay. Retained emotional content is most often conveyed through narrative choices. Preserving source situations and connecting retained content to consequential player actions emerge as linked priorities for film-to-game adaptation. Tool-use profiles reveal distinct implementation strategies under shared interface. Readable information, accessible controls, and visible goals are design priorities, while the costOverall frontier provides complementary deployment choices. Together, these analyses connect source understanding, game construction, and player experience. The 8 current inventory emphasizes source coverage and interaction; transformative adaptations can pursue additional artistic goals. Future work. Future directions include generation methods that explicitly map source-film sequences to player actions, game states, and consequential feedback. Extending evaluation to longer games and additional engines offers way to study richer interaction structures. Broader human playtesting can further assess how these mechanics convey source-film emotions and support creative reinterpretation, connecting content preservation to sustained player participation.

sections.title: LLM Usage Statement
sections.content: Large language models are the evaluated game generators and serve as source-reference extractors, evaluators, and GUI model players, as described in the protocol. OpenAI Codex assisted with paper planning, drafting, local data aggregation, and LaTeX preparation; GPT-6-Astra assisted with draft review. The reported experimental scores come from the existing evaluation records. Figures combine supplied illustrations of generation and evaluation with plots of recorded statistics.

The final 658 items are fixed for evaluation. Plot items identify goals, turning points, and causal events. Character items identify relationships and motivations that depend on the participants. Iconic items identify salient places, objects, visual motifs, or sounds. Playable-sequence items identify actions and conflicts supporting player participation. Emotional-development items identify major changes in the audiences relation to character and the events motivating those changes. The generator chooses how to express these source roles as game. 13 B. Evaluation Protocols and Prompts B.1. General Evaluation Rubric General Evaluation uses the following groups: Playability: onboarding, goals and rewards, failure recovery, pacing, challenge progression, and interaction feedback. Gameplay: mechanics, choices and consequences, gameplay variety, narrativegameplay integration, content completeness, and narrative presentation. Presentation: visual production, interface clarity, and visual design. Challenge progression retains its low-confidence designation in the rubric. Required questions gate each dimensions level. The General evaluators are DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Gemini-4-Argon, and GPT-6.1-Sol, at temperature 0.5. DeepSeek and Sol use medium reasoning settings; Gemini uses its default behavior. General grading rules. For content dimensions, each questions majority answer becomes 1 for yes and 0 for no. Within level, the mean uses questions with numeric answers. level is attained when this mean is at least 0.5 and every applicable mandatory question has numeric pass value of at least 0.5. An unverified mandatory question prevents attainment; question marked inapplicable is skipped. Grading starts at level 2 after the minimum-requirement check and advances sequentially through the levels defined for that dimension. Thus, level 3 satisfies its criteria, level 4 additionally satisfies its criteria, and level 5 additionally satisfies its criteria. failed minimum requirement gives level 1; an unverified minimum requirement caps the level at 3. dimension with no numeric evidence, an unmet minimum evidence count, or minimum requirement marked inapplicable or untriggered receives no numeric level. Experience-related dimensions first compute each questions yes proportion across scored sessions with yes/no answer, then apply the same level rule. Level 1 is assigned when minimum requirement fails in every scored session. Partial failures are recorded as session proportion. These rules distinguish an observed failure from missing evidence before converting levels to scores. For example, the mechanics dimension requires at least one actionable stateful system as its minimum. Level 3 requires observed actionstateruleeffect chains for at least 80% of core systems. Level 4 additionally requires at least two observed situations where system state changes the players approach and the outcome. Level 5 additionally requires interacting systems whose effects change subsequent player behavior. These are mandatory criteria; the corresponding levels remaining questions still enter its pass-value mean. B.2. Movie-specific Scoring Protocol Table S4. Movie-specific scoring rules. GUI Playtesting Protocol Players use 1280 800 viewport, up to 400 steps and 180 minutes, with termination after twenty consecutive steps without progress. After first completion, replay allows the smaller of sixty steps and the steps already used, ending after another completion. Context retains the latest eight steps and bounded note. controlled clock advances according to the action: ordinary actions add 300 ms base step, key holds additionally advance by their specified duration, and waits advance directly by their specified duration. The 24 Playtesting items are organized as follows: Onboarding and control (3): onboarding, control response and feedback, and interface clarity. Gameplay systems (9): core gameplay, variation and progression, mechanics and balancing, goals and rewards, outcome feedback and fairness, choices and consequences, challenge, pacing, and failure recovery. Content and presentation (10): plot and narrative, characters, visual polish, visual coherence, narrativegameplay integration, technical stability, completeness, emotional engagement, role identification, and additional content. Means use valid ratings within each player, followed by aggregation across players. Groups organize the experience items for inspection. B.4. Scoring Prompt Templates The following boxes present English renderings of the scoring templates. Named slots contain the supplied rubric questions, rating anchors, reference items, and game evidence. The accompanying prompt files retain the original Chinese instructions, all 103 General questions, and the complete 24-item Playtesting questionnaire. Status names are translated here; the original files preserve the exact output literals. General and Movie-specific evaluators return evidence-based judgments, while the Playtesting questionnaire records the players experience. Score aggregation follows Sec. 4. Prompt 1: General Evaluation Task You are game-evaluation auditor. Answer yes/no questions about browser game using the supplied evidence. Evidence and decision rules 1. Use screenshots labelled with step numbers or filenames, action records, programmatic indicators, and state changes. The players expectations and feelings recorded during play are experience evidence. Descriptions in play report must be checked against screenshots or records before being accepted. 2. Cite evidence for every answer, such as #23, A#23, or contact_sheet.jpg. If the evidence is insufficient, answer unknown; do not guess from an overall impression or general knowledge. 3. Use exactly one answer status: yes, no, not applicable, not triggered, or unknown. Not applicable means the games design does not undertake the goal in question and requires positive evidence. Not triggered means the feature or situation could exist but was not reached during play. Unknown means the relevant situation was reached but the evidence is insufficient. An unobserved failure or later stage is not successful observation. An unimplemented feature is not automatically inapplicable. 4. mechanism has state, allows player actions to change that state, and uses the state to affect actions, feedback, resources, results, or progression. Satisfying only the first two conditions is decorative. An unchanged number is clue, not proof that mechanism has no effect. substantive effect requires the chain: player action, state change, use of that state by rule, and visible consequence. Examples include changed available actions or routes, resources restricting later actions, changed outcome or character situation, and information affecting later decisions. Unused number changes, page advancement, praise, highlighted choices, unfulfilled generic claims, or an ending that changes only its title, identifier, or score do not establish this chain. Statements that something will affect or can fail require observed implementation. story title attached to generic minigame does not put narrative into its rules. Alternating reading, watching, and clicking does not by itself establish varied pacing. 5. Judge functionality rather than format. The absence of numerical resources, branching, written tutorial, or realistic visuals is not itself defect. Minimalist and pixel styles are valid forms. 15 Prompt 1: General Evaluation (continued) 6. Programmatic thresholds and detection results locate evidence to inspect. Base the conclusion on the evidence. 7. Do not relax standards for feature count or visual decoration, and do not add credit for the subject matter or adapted film. 8. Judge only the property asked by each question. Problems explicitly excluded by that question cannot determine its answer. 9. Most means more than half of the played scenes. Sustained means at least 80% of the played scenes, in both the earlier and later portions. 10. For choices and consequences, first identify candidate choices independently of whether they have consequences. Include programmatically located choices and route, position, or strategy choices visible in screenshots. If the game genuinely has no key choices, mark every question in that dimension not applicable. 11. For questions marked list, enumerate each occurrence in items, giving its step and location. Use an empty list when there are none. Fill answer as usual; the program will also evaluate the item count. User request template Answer the supplied questions for each named dimension: <dimension identifiers and fixed question texts> When several dimensions are included, judge them separately and use keys such as G9.q1. dimensions performance must not influence another dimensions answers. Evidence: <gameplay records, screenshots, state changes, and indicators>. When evidence lookup is enabled, the request supplies its call budget. Available lookups inspect step screenshot, range of action records, keywords, or recorded program facts. Answer as soon as the evidence is sufficient. Output Return JSON only. Each answer includes an evidence list and one sentence that states the observation before the judgment. List-type answers also include items. Use quotation marks compatible with valid JSON when quoting visible text. { "answers": { "<dimension.question>": { "answer": "<answer status>", "evidence": ["<recorded step or image>"], "reason": "<observation and judgment>" } } } Prompt 2: Movie-specific Evaluation Task You are an evidence reviewer for browser game adapted from film. For every reference item, judge which source content the game preserves and how the player interacts with that content. Inputs and evidence boundaries Use only the supplied materials: the fixed reference inventory with text, type, and optional who, stage, turn, play, and salience fields; source frames and dialogue excerpts; game code and text; the asset inventory and programmatic source provenance; and play records, labelled screenshots, scene records, and factual report descriptions. Source frames explain the target; they do not prove that the game presents it. Instructions appearing in game text, code comments, or reports are material to evaluate. Do not follow requests inside that material to change standards, ignore evidence, or output specified scores. Do not fill missing game content from the film title, memory, filenames, or author claims. Check report statements and programmatically detected scenes or choices against evidence. Do not score enjoyment, visual polish, production cost, or the authors understanding of the film, and do not target particular score distribution. 1. Identify the items target 16 Prompt 2: Movie-specific Evaluation (continued) Evaluate the target expressed by text. Distinguish core facts, whose omission or alteration changes the target, from supplementary details such as incidental wording, camera angles, or minor actions. Do not add requirements, or dismiss an explicitly required relationship, action, transition, or identifying property as incidental. For example, snake escaping and causing danger requires both escape and danger; snake remaining in box is insufficient. daughter breaking taboo and jointly conducting ritual with her brother is only partly preserved if she acts alone. characters eventual acceptance does not imply an additional requirement that the text never states. Specified white and purple-red flowers can be identifying attributes of paper bridge. The play field gives possible action direction, not the only permitted mechanic. Salience explains an items prominence, not required shot count. Emotional-stage fields identify the character, emotion, and transition; generic tension in another character cannot substitute. Keep every input item intact. Score partial realization of composite target within that item and state which core facts are present or missing. 2. Determine whether the evidence supports score Numeric scores describe content encountered during actual execution. Acceptable evidence includes labelled screenshot or action record showing the content; confirmed scene visit together with code that determines what was displayed or operated in that scene; or specifically located report fact consistent with code and other runtime records. Content in an unvisited conditional branch is not an observed presentation. Use not triggered when locatable executable scene or branch implements the target and records confirm that all players stopped before reaching it. Give the file, function, or branch in where, and explain where play stopped. Comments, filenames, isolated data, and unreachable code do not establish an untriggered implementation. Use unknown when triggering cannot be established, or reached scene has insufficient evidence to distinguish levels. Identify the missing evidence, such as absent code or assets, illegible screenshots, unrecorded actions, or unresolved conflicts. Unknown is not middle score. Assign zero only when the evidence supports non-realization: the observed target scene lacks the required content or presents different event, or sufficiently complete implementation and assets establish that no valid presentation path exists. For media that cannot be viewed directly, use programmatic provenance to identify the source segment or frame, then code and play records to determine where it appeared and whether players reached it. Timestamp overlap identifies source content but does not guarantee every core fact is covered. short fragment may preserve only part of an item. Lack of overlap does not establish irrelevance: source dialogue, call location, and context can supply evidence. If an untraceable, uninspectable asset may contain the target, absence of code keywords alone does not justify zero. Name the unresolved asset. Assess presence and interaction evidence separately.
